CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and inflammation -> Recruitment and polarization of TAMs with high TGF-β signaling -> Establishment of an immunosuppressive TME -> Dual-targeting nanoparticles deliver high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 to TAMs -> Disruption of TGF-βR signaling in TAMs -> Reprogramming from M2 (immunosuppressive) to M1 (pro-inflammatory) phenotype -> Enhanced antigen presentation and effector T-cell activation -> Improved efficacy of conventional immunotherapies in HCC
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that leveraging a refined therapeutic strategy—which employs dual-targeting, multi-ligand nanoparticles for the precise delivery of high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 systems to tumor-associated macrophages in HCC—will effectively disrupt TGF-β receptor signaling. This targeted disruption is predicted to reprogram TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype. The consequent enhancement in antigen presentation and effector T-cell activation is expected to synergistically boost the efficacy of conventional immunotherapies. To mitigate translational challenges, our approach integrates inducible safety switches and comprehensive preclinical monitoring protocols that assess nanoparticle biodistribution, gene editing efficiency, and immune modulation.
Abstract: This study proposes an advanced therapeutic strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that refines a TAM-centric gene-editing approach by integrating dual-targeting, multi-ligand nanoparticles with high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 systems. Building on the established causal chain—from chronic liver injury and inflammation to TAM polarization and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment—our approach aims to selectively disrupt TGF-β receptor (TGF-βR) signaling in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). This targeted gene editing is expected to reprogram TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing antigen presentation and T-cell activation and synergizing with conventional immunotherapies. Key enhancements include advanced ligand-directed nanoparticle design for improved targeting specificity, inducible safety switches to prevent off-target effects, and rigorous preclinical monitoring of gene-editing efficiency, biodistribution, and immune response dynamics. This integrated strategy addresses previous translational challenges while preserving and extending the original mechanistic rationale.

It advances the original concept by incorporating modern technological enhancements such as dual-targeting, multi-ligand nanoparticle design for improved specificity, detailed safety switches to reduce off-target effects, and thorough preclinical monitoring protocols.
